newsitem.title: USA: Republicans see some optimism on budget front.
newsitem.headline: Republicans see some optimism on budget front.

text.p: Republican budget leaders expressed cautious optimism on Thursday that talks with President Bill Clinton and his Democrats would result in a balanced budget and warned political strife lay ahead if they failed.

"If we don't reach accord with the president, he can look forward to a very frustrating couple of years," Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici said in a speech on the Senate floor. The New Mexico Republican said talks would continue in the next couple of weeks on the staff level, as requested by Clinton during a White House meeting on Wednesday.
"I truly believe there is a possibility this could work," Domenici said of the chances this new effort to balance the budget by 2002 would yield a compromise.
Just in case it should fail he took a procedural step to pave the way for debate on a bare-bones budget and on the president's plan, neither of which the veteran budget writer said he supported.
But Democratic leaders blamed Republicans who control Congress for the slow progress and chided them for not producing a budget to counter Clinton's plan.

The president proposed a way to cut taxes and reduce spending growth that would bring the budget to a $17 billion surplus by 2002. Republicans, using the Congressional Budget Office economic forecasts, charged Clinton would leave a $69 billion deficit that year. They have said Clinton should send up a new balanced budget, which the administration replied is unnecessary.

"It is impossible to see anything happening other than gridlock, and maybe even shutting the government down, because we can't do the work that we were sent here to do," House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, Democrat of Missouri, told reporters.
In the House, Republicans were still in turmoil over House Speaker Newt Gingrich's suggestion that they set aside a key party goal of cutting taxes until the budget is balanced.

House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich asserted that the final budget will include tax cuts and a proposal he would offer if negotiations fail would include tax relief. He said he felt strongly that a Republican party that could produce a budget without tax cuts was "a Republican party that is in danger of losing its soul."

A bipartisan group of 56 House lawmakers signed a letter to Gingrich supporting his suggestion that tax cuts be separate from the budget. This countered a letter from 28 Republicans urging him to fight for the Republican tax cut.

Republicans said they were not concerned that they would miss the April 15 deadline to approve a budget and Kasich said he did not respond to what he called a "nasty letter" from Democrats chiding the slow progres. "At some point we are going to be able to get serious work done. There's no deadlines here. They really ought to relax," Kasich said.
